theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: How does a hydroxide relaxer straighten hair?
options: It breaks bonds in the cortex so the curl can be smoothed straight
It coats the cuticle with a heavy oil that weighs the curl down
It dries the hair out so that it cannot hold a curl
It stretches the hair with heat until the curl is gone for a while

questions.stem: What is lanthionisation?
options: The change of bonds that a hydroxide relaxer makes in the hair
The rinsing step done straight after the relaxer is fully applied
A test for metallic salts in the hair
The colour change shown by an indicator shampoo

questions.stem: Why is a hydroxide relaxer dangerous to skin and eyes?
options: It is very acidic, like vinegar
It is neutral, like plain water
It is very alkaline, with a high pH
It is very cold when it comes out of the jar

questions.stem: What does a 'no-lye' relaxer usually contain?
options: Sodium hydroxide only
Guanidine hydroxide, made by mixing a cream with an activator
Hydrogen peroxide and ammonia
Ammonium thioglycolate mixed with a liquid oxidising neutraliser

questions.stem: When should the activator be mixed into a no-lye relaxer cream?
options: The night before, so that it is ready
After the relaxer is on the hair
Never, because the two parts are always applied one after the other
Just before use, as the maker's instructions say

questions.stem: A client's hair was straightened with a thio (thioglycolate) product. What is true about putting a hydroxide relaxer on it?
options: It is safe if the hydroxide is a mild strength
It is safe if you leave it on for half the time
It is safe after one deep conditioning treatment
The two do not mix; it can cause severe breakage

questions.stem: Which relaxer strength is usually chosen for fine, porous or colour-treated hair, if the maker allows it at all?
options: Super
Mild
Regular
Extra super

questions.stem: How do you decide which relaxer strength and timing to use?
options: From the hair analysis, the strand test and the maker's instructions
Always use the strongest one in the salon so that the hair is straight faster
Use whatever the last client had
Ask the client which jar looks nicest

questions.stem: Why must you ask about past chemical services and home products before a relaxer?
options: To decide what music she likes
So that you can charge for each one
Some treatments react badly with relaxers or weaken the hair
Because past chemical services always make the new relaxer much cheaper

questions.stem: Before a relaxer, you find small scratches and scabs (abrasions) on the scalp. What should you do?
options: Cover them with plenty of extra base cream and then carry on
Do not relax today; rebook when the scalp has healed
Use a no-lye relaxer, as it is safe on cuts
Apply the relaxer quickly so it does not sting

questions.stem: Why should the client not scratch her scalp, or have it brushed hard, before a relaxer?
options: It makes the hair grow faster
It removes the natural curl
It makes the relaxer smell much stronger in the room
It can break the skin, so the relaxer may burn

questions.stem: Why is the hair usually not shampooed just before a hydroxide relaxer?
options: So that the relaxer will smell less
So that the hair stays dirty and grips the relaxer cream better
The scalp's natural oil helps protect it from the chemical
Because shampoo makes the relaxer stronger

questions.stem: Which tests should be done before a relaxer?
options: The skin and strand tests the maker requires, plus porosity and elasticity
Only a check that the client can pay
A test of how long the client can sit
No tests, because relaxers are safe for everyone

questions.stem: What does a strand test before a relaxer tell you?
options: How the hair reacts and roughly how long it needs
Whether the client likes the smell of the relaxer
How much the client's hair will grow next month
Which colour the client's hair will turn

questions.stem: The hair snaps easily and does not spring back in an elasticity test. What should you advise?
options: Use a super relaxer to make it stronger
Relax it twice to make sure it is straight
Do not relax it now; give conditioning treatments first
Relax it today and then blow-dry it straight with high heat

questions.stem: Why is an incompatibility test done if a client may have used a home dye with metallic salts or a henna compound?
options: To check how long she has used the dye
To see whether the dye colour matches her skin tone and eyes
To find out how much the dye cost
Because these can react with chemicals and damage the hair

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the protective base cream in a relaxer service?
options: To make the relaxer work faster and more strongly on the hair
To protect the scalp, hairline and ears from the chemical
To add shine to the finished hair
To colour the new growth

questions.stem: With a 'base' relaxer, where is the protective base applied?
options: Only on the ends of the hair
Only on the ears
Over the whole scalp, the hairline and the ears
On the stylist's hands and arms instead of wearing gloves

questions.stem: With a 'no-base' relaxer, what protection is still needed?
options: Base cream on the hairline and ears, and around any sensitive area
None at all, because no-base relaxers are too mild to ever burn the skin
Only a towel on the shoulders
Cotton wool in the client's ears only

questions.stem: What should the stylist wear when applying a relaxer?
options: Thin cotton gloves and short sleeves
Chemical-resistant gloves and a protective apron, as the maker says
No gloves, so that she can feel the hair
Rubber boots and a hat

questions.stem: Why must the salon be well ventilated during chemical straightening?
options: To keep the relaxer cold
To dry the client's hair much faster after the rinse is done
To make the client feel cooler
To carry away fumes that can irritate eyes and breathing

questions.stem: On a virgin relaxer (hair that has never been relaxed), where is the relaxer usually applied first?
options: On the fine hair at the front hairline
On the ends only
On the most resistant area, often at the back
Straight onto the scalp all over the head at once

questions.stem: On a virgin relaxer, why is the product kept a short distance off the scalp at first?
options: So that the relaxer smells less
Body heat makes hair near the scalp process faster
So that the roots stay curly
Because the scalp itself does not need any protecting

questions.stem: Why is the hairline usually relaxed last?
options: The hair there is often finer and processes faster
The hair there is always the strongest
The client cannot see that part of her head in the mirror
It is the easiest part to reach

questions.stem: During a relaxer retouch, where should the relaxer go?
options: On all the hair, from roots to ends
On the ends, to keep them straight
On the relaxed hair first, then the new growth
On the new growth only

questions.stem: Why must relaxer never be overlapped onto hair that was relaxed before?
options: It makes the new growth curly again
It wastes product and costs the salon a lot more money
It turns the hair a lighter colour
It over-processes the hair, which then breaks

questions.stem: How can you protect previously relaxed hair during a retouch?
options: Apply a protective cream or conditioner to it, as the maker says
Wet it with plenty of hot water
Cover it with more relaxer
Brush it hard to close the cuticle

questions.stem: How should the hair be smoothed while the relaxer is processing?
options: Pull the hair hard and fast with a fine-tooth comb from root to end
Gently, with the back of the comb, a brush or gloved hands
Rub the scalp hard to work the relaxer in
Leave it alone the whole time

questions.stem: How long should a relaxer stay on the hair?
options: Until the client says it is burning
Twice as long as the maker says, to be sure
No longer than the maker's instructions say, timed from the start
Until the stylist finishes another client

questions.stem: Why do you start the timer when you begin applying the relaxer?
options: Processing begins as soon as the relaxer touches the hair
So that the client knows when to pay
Because the relaxer only starts to work once a timer has been set
So that you can take a break

questions.stem: During processing, the client says her scalp is burning. What should you do?
options: Tell her it means the relaxer is working
Fan the area with a towel and keep going until the timer has ended
Add base cream on top of the relaxer
Rinse the relaxer off that area at once with plenty of water

questions.stem: How should the relaxer be rinsed out?
options: Quickly with cold water for a few seconds, then shampoo
With a damp towel, wiping from the ends
Thoroughly with warm water until no relaxer is left
With conditioner only and no water

questions.stem: Why should the rinse water be directed away from the client's face?
options: So that her make-up does not run
To stop relaxer getting into her eyes
To keep the shampoo basin clean and free of hair
So that the water stays warm

questions.stem: What does a neutralising (normalising) shampoo do after a hydroxide relaxer?
options: It makes the new growth curly again so that it matches the ends
It stops the chemical action and brings the pH back to normal
It adds colour to the new growth
It speeds up the relaxer

questions.stem: A colour-indicator neutralising shampoo changes colour while you lather. What does this show?
options: The shampoo is old and should be thrown away
The client is allergic to the shampoo
Relaxer is still in the hair, so keep shampooing as the maker says
The hair is ready to be coloured

questions.stem: After a thio (thioglycolate) straightener, what is used to rebuild the bonds in the new straight shape?
options: A neutralising shampoo for hydroxide relaxers
A protein conditioner
Hot water only
An oxidising neutraliser, as the maker says

questions.stem: What should be applied after neutralising and before styling?
options: A conditioner suited to chemically treated hair
A second coat of relaxer
A permanent colour
Heavy grease rubbed into the scalp to stop it drying out

questions.stem: How should freshly relaxed hair be dried and styled?
options: Gently, with low to medium heat and little tension
With the hottest flat iron pressed close to the scalp
By rubbing hard with a towel to dry it fast
By pulling it into a very tight ponytail

questions.stem: Relaxer splashes into a client's eye. What should you do?
options: Wipe it with a dry tissue and carry on
Put a drop of conditioner in the eye
Rinse with plenty of clean running water for a long time and get medical help
Tell her to keep the eye shut until the service ends

questions.stem: A chemical burn appears on the scalp after a relaxer. What should you do?
options: Cover it with grease and say nothing
Rinse with cool water, record it, report it and advise medical help
Apply more neutralising shampoo to it
Pick off any scab to help it heal

questions.stem: How should relaxers be stored?
options: Open, so they do not go hard
In a warm place near the hood dryers so that they stay soft and smooth
Mixed together in one tub
Closed and labelled, in a cool, dry place out of reach

questions.stem: What should you do with leftover mixed no-lye relaxer at the end of the service?
options: Keep it in the fridge for the next client
Add it to a new jar of relaxer so that nothing is wasted
Pour it down the basin with no water
Throw it away as the maker's instructions say

questions.stem: A client with natural coily hair wants only to loosen her curl pattern, not straighten it. Which service suits this?
options: A full super-strength relaxer
A texturiser, used as the maker says
A permanent colour with a strong developer
A hot oil treatment

questions.stem: A client asks if her relaxed hair will go back to its natural coily pattern. What is true?
options: Yes, after three shampoos
Yes, after a deep conditioning treatment
No; relaxed hair stays straight, and only new growth is natural
Yes, if she wets it with sea water

questions.stem: Which aftercare advice should you give after a relaxer?
options: Do not scratch the scalp, condition often, and retouch only the new growth
Relax the hair again next week to keep it straight
Use the hottest flat iron every day
Wear very tight styles to keep it flat

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe the consultation and tests you carry out before a relaxer, and say what would stop you going ahead.
essays.modelAnswer: I sit with the client in good light and ask what result she wants, when her last relaxer was, which product was used, and about colour, henna, home dyes, heat and other chemical services. I ask about allergies, past reactions, medical conditions and whether she has scratched or brushed her scalp hard recently. I part the hair and check the whole scalp and hairline for abrasions, cuts, sores, redness or infection. I check the hair's porosity, elasticity, texture and density, and how much new growth there is. I do the skin and strand tests the maker requires, and an incompatibility test if she may have used metallic dyes or henna compounds. I would not go ahead if the scalp has any abrasions or sores, if the skin test is positive, if the hair has poor elasticity or is badly damaged, if the strand test shows breakage, if metallic salts are found, or if the hair was treated with a thio product. I record everything and agree the plan.
markingPoints: Asks about past relaxers, colour, henna, home products and reactions
Checks the scalp and hairline for abrasions, cuts, sores or infection
Checks porosity, elasticity, texture, density and new growth
Skin and strand tests as the maker requires; incompatibility test where needed
Names correct reasons to stop, and records the consultation

essays.stem: Explain how hydroxide relaxers and thio straighteners work, and why the two must never be used on the same hair.
essays.modelAnswer: Hair gets much of its strength and curl from disulphide bonds in the cortex. A hydroxide relaxer, such as sodium hydroxide (lye) or guanidine hydroxide (no-lye), is very alkaline. It swells the hair, enters the cortex and breaks some of the disulphide bonds, which change into new bonds (lanthionisation). The hair is smoothed straight, and the change is permanent; a neutralising shampoo then stops the chemical action and returns the pH to normal. A thio straightener uses ammonium thioglycolate. It also breaks disulphide bonds, but in a different way, and the hair is then treated with an oxidising neutraliser, which rebuilds the bonds in the new straight shape. Because the two work in different ways, putting one on hair already treated with the other can cause the hair to break off badly. So I always ask which product was used, check the record card, and never apply hydroxide over thio-treated hair or thio over hydroxide-treated hair.
markingPoints: Disulphide bonds in the cortex give strength and curl
Hydroxide relaxers are very alkaline and break bonds permanently (lanthionisation)
Neutralising shampoo stops the action and returns pH to normal
Thio straighteners break bonds and are rebuilt with an oxidising neutraliser
The two are incompatible; using one over the other causes severe breakage, so history is checked

essays.stem: Describe how you prepare and protect the client, the scalp and the hairline before applying a relaxer.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that the consultation and the tests the maker requires have been done and recorded. I do not shampoo the hair before a hydroxide relaxer, because the scalp's natural oil helps protect it. I check the scalp again for abrasions; if there are any, I stop. I gown the client, put a fresh towel and a waterproof chemical cape around her shoulders, and make sure clothing is covered. I make sure the area is well ventilated. I divide the dry hair into four sections and clip them. For a base relaxer, I apply protective base cream over the whole scalp, the hairline and the ears, as the maker says. For a no-base relaxer, I still apply base to the hairline, ears and any sensitive areas. I protect the fine edges carefully. If it is a retouch, I protect the previously relaxed hair with the protective cream or conditioner the maker says. I put on chemical-resistant gloves and an apron, set out a timer, and keep water ready at the basin.
markingPoints: Tests done; no shampoo before a hydroxide relaxer; scalp re-checked for abrasions
Client gowned with towel and chemical cape; area ventilated
Hair sectioned dry into four
Base cream applied correctly for base and no-base relaxers, including hairline, edges and ears
Previously relaxed hair protected on a retouch; gloves, apron and timer ready

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to apply a virgin relaxer, including smoothing and timing.
essays.modelAnswer: After the consultation, tests and protection, I put on gloves and divide the hair into four sections. I start the timer as soon as the relaxer first touches the hair, because processing begins at once. I begin in the most resistant area, often at the back of the head. I take thin partings and apply the relaxer to both sides of each parting, starting a short distance from the scalp, as the maker's instructions say, and working out to just before the ends, which are more porous. I work quickly and neatly through each section. Then I go back and apply the relaxer to the hair near the scalp, which processes faster because of body heat, and finally to the ends. The fine hairline is done last. I smooth each section gently with the back of the comb, an applicator brush or my gloved hands, never pulling. I check the curl reduction with a strand test during processing and rinse before the maker's time is up, or at once if the client feels burning.
markingPoints: Gloves on, four sections, timer started at first application
Starts at the most resistant area, thin partings, a short distance from the scalp, as the maker says
Scalp area and ends applied afterwards; hairline last
Gentle smoothing without pulling
Checks with a strand test and rinses within the maker's time, or at once if burning

essays.stem: Describe how to carry out a relaxer retouch, and explain why relaxer must never be overlapped onto previously relaxed hair.
essays.modelAnswer: A retouch treats only the new growth that has come out since the last relaxer. I check the record card for the last product and date, and check the scalp for abrasions. I make sure there is enough new growth to work on safely, as the maker's instructions say. I protect the scalp, hairline and ears with base cream, and I coat the previously relaxed hair with the protective cream or conditioner the maker says. I divide the hair into four sections, start the timer and apply the relaxer to the new growth only, starting in the most resistant area and keeping it a short distance from the scalp, as the maker says. I take care to stop at the line of demarcation and not touch the relaxed hair. I smooth gently and rinse within the maker's time. Relaxer must never overlap onto hair that was relaxed before, because those bonds are already broken. More relaxer over-processes it, making it weak, limp and likely to break off at the line of demarcation.
markingPoints: Treats new growth only; checks record card and scalp first
Protects scalp, hairline and previously relaxed hair as the maker says
Applies to new growth only, stopping at the line of demarcation
Gentle smoothing and timing within the maker's instructions
Explains that overlapping over-processes the hair and causes breakage

essays.stem: Explain the steps after processing: rinsing, neutralising (normalising) shampoo and conditioning, and why each step matters.
essays.modelAnswer: When the processing time is up, or sooner if the hair is straight enough or the client feels stinging, I take the client to the basin. I rinse the hair thoroughly with warm water and a strong flow, keeping the hair straight and directing the water away from her face and eyes, until all the relaxer is gone. Rinsing well stops most of the chemical action and prevents burns. Then I use the neutralising (normalising) shampoo the maker says. It is acid-balanced, so it stops the action of any relaxer left in the hair and brings the hair and scalp back towards a normal pH. If the shampoo has a colour indicator, I lather and rinse as many times as the maker says, until it shows no relaxer is left. Missing this step can let the relaxer keep working and damage the hair and scalp. Finally I apply a conditioner for chemically treated hair, as the maker says, to restore moisture and smooth the cuticle, then rinse and style gently with low heat.
markingPoints: Thorough rinse with warm water, hair kept straight, water away from face
Rinsing removes the relaxer and stops most action
Neutralising shampoo is acid-balanced, stops action and restores pH
Repeats as the maker says, using the colour indicator if present
Conditions treated hair and styles gently

essays.stem: A client with natural, coily hair is thinking about a relaxer. Explain the choices she has and the advice you would give.
essays.modelAnswer: I first find out why she wants a change, for example easier combing, a sleeker style or less shrinkage, and look at her hair's condition, texture, density and porosity. I explain that a relaxer is permanent: the treated hair will stay straight, and her natural pattern will only return in the new growth, which will need retouches. If she wants only a looser curl, a texturiser used as the maker says may suit her. If she is unsure, she could try a non-chemical option first, such as a silk press or blow-dry with heat protection, or protective styles such as twists or braids that are not too tight. I explain the care relaxed hair needs: regular deep conditioning, gentle handling, low heat and retouches on new growth only. If her hair is weak or damaged, I advise treatments before any chemical. If she later wants to return to natural hair, transitioning needs gentle care at the line of demarcation. I respect her choice and record the advice.
markingPoints: Finds out her reasons and analyses the hair
Explains that relaxing is permanent and only new growth is natural
Offers options: texturiser, non-chemical styling, protective styles
Explains the care relaxed hair needs and treatments first if the hair is weak
Respects her choice and records the advice

essays.stem: Explain how relaxers and straightening products should be handled, stored and disposed of safely.
essays.modelAnswer: Relaxers are strong, very alkaline chemicals that can burn skin, eyes and scalp, so I follow the maker's instructions, the safety data sheet and the Centre's rules every time. I wear chemical-resistant gloves and an apron, and eye protection if the maker says, and I protect the client with a gown, towel and chemical cape. The salon must be well ventilated. I never mix brands or products, and I never put a thio product on hydroxide-relaxed hair or the other way round. For no-lye relaxers, I mix the activator only just before use, as the maker says, and throw away what is left. Products are stored in their original, labelled containers, tightly closed, in a cool, dry place away from heat and sunlight, out of the reach of children, and used before the expiry date. I wipe up spills at once with gloves on. Used gloves, applicators and leftover product are disposed of as the maker and the Centre's rules say, and tools and bowls are washed, then disinfected.
markingPoints: Follows maker's instructions, SDS and Centre's rules; knows the chemicals burn
Correct PPE for stylist and client; good ventilation
Never mixes brands or incompatible products; activator mixed just before use
Stored labelled, closed, cool, dry, out of reach, in date
Spills wiped with gloves; waste disposed of as the rules say; tools cleaned and disinfected

essays.stem: Describe what you would do if relaxer got into a client's eye, if the scalp was burned, and if you noticed the hair breaking during a service.
essays.modelAnswer: If relaxer gets into an eye, I act at once. I hold the eyelid open and rinse the eye with plenty of clean, cool running water, from the inside corner outwards, for at least 15 minutes or as long as the SDS says, and I do not let the client rub it. I call for help and get medical attention, taking the product label or SDS with us. If the scalp burns or stings during processing, I rinse the relaxer off that area at once with plenty of cool to lukewarm water, then use the neutralising shampoo gently as the maker says. I do not put grease on a burn or pick at it. I advise the client to see a doctor if the skin is broken, blistered or very sore. If I see the hair breaking or becoming gummy, I stop and rinse at once, neutralise and condition. In every case I tell my supervisor, fill in the accident or incident report, record it on the record card, and do not relax that hair again until it has recovered.
markingPoints: Eye: rinse at once with plenty of clean running water for the SDS time, no rubbing, medical help
Burn: rinse the area at once, neutralise gently, no grease, refer if blistered or broken
Breakage: stop, rinse, neutralise and condition at once
Reports to supervisor and completes an incident report
Records it and does not re-relax until the hair and scalp recover

essays.stem: Describe the aftercare advice you give after a relaxer, and what you record on the client's record card.
essays.modelAnswer: I tell the client not to scratch her scalp and to wait before shampooing again, as the maker says. I advise a gentle shampoo and conditioner for relaxed hair, regular deep conditioning or protein-and-moisture treatments, and a leave-in conditioner. I suggest she avoids high heat and uses a heat protector, and that she avoids tight ponytails, braids and weaves that pull on the edges. I advise her to sleep with her hair wrapped in a satin scarf and to protect it from sun, sea water and chlorine. I explain that any colour service must wait as long as the maker says. I tell her to come back for a retouch on the new growth only, when there is enough new growth, and never to relax at home over relaxed hair. I ask her to contact the salon if the scalp becomes sore. On the record card I write the date, product and strength, test results, scalp condition, the areas treated, the processing time, the neutralising steps, the result and the advice given.
markingPoints: No scratching; gentle shampoo and conditioner; regular conditioning treatments
Low heat with protection; no tight styles; satin scarf; protect from sun and sea water
Colour only after the time the maker says; retouch new growth only
Contact the salon if the scalp is sore
Records date, product, strength, tests, scalp condition, timing, neutralising and result

practical1.title: Relaxer retouch on new growth, with a training head
practical1.brief: As a group, carry out a full relaxer retouch on a training head (mannequin) that has relaxed hair with natural new growth at the roots. Treat the training head exactly as a real client. One member leads the consultation as a role play with another member playing the client, while the group fills in the record card: past relaxers and product type, colour or henna, scalp check for abrasions, porosity and elasticity, and the skin and strand tests the maker requires. Then each member takes one of the four sections and, while the assessor watches, applies base cream to the hairline, edges and ears for that section, coats the previously relaxed hair with protective cream as the maker says, and applies relaxer to the new growth only without overlapping. One member keeps the timer from the first application. Smooth gently, rinse thoroughly, use the neutralising shampoo as the maker says, condition and finish. Photograph each stage (hair and hands only) and hand in the record card with the photos.
materials: Training head with relaxed hair and new growth at the roots, on a clamp
Relaxer for retouch use, with the maker's instructions and SDS
Protective base cream and protective cream or conditioner for relaxed hair
Neutralising (normalising) shampoo and a conditioner for chemically treated hair
Chemical-resistant gloves, aprons, chemical capes and towels
Tint bowl, applicator brush, tail comb, sectioning clips and a timer
photos: The station set up, with members in gloves and aprons and the record card filled in
The hair divided into four sections
Base cream on the hairline, edges and ears
Protective cream on the previously relaxed hair
Relaxer on the new growth only, with the line of demarcation visible
The neutralising shampoo lather at the basin
The finished, conditioned and styled result, and the cleaned station
checklist: Took part in the consultation and checked for thio, henna or metallic dye history
Checked the scalp for abrasions and recorded the tests the maker requires
Wore chemical-resistant gloves and an apron and protected the client area
Applied base cream to the hairline, edges and ears
Protected the previously relaxed hair as the maker says
Applied relaxer to the new growth only, with no overlap onto relaxed hair
Smoothed gently and kept to the maker's timing, from the first application
Rinsed thoroughly, used neutralising shampoo as the maker says, conditioned and cleaned up safely
safety: Follow the maker's instructions, the SDS and the Centre's rules; never mix brands
Wear chemical-resistant gloves and an apron; keep the area ventilated
On a real client, never relax over abrasions, cuts or sores; rinse at once if the scalp burns
Know where the eyewash and clean running water are; rinse eyes at once and get help
Store relaxers closed and labelled; wipe spills at once with gloves on

practical2.title: Virgin relaxer or texturiser on natural, textured hair, with a training head
practical2.brief: As a group, carry out a virgin relaxer or texturiser application on a training head with natural, coily hair that has never been chemically treated. Treat the training head as a real client. Together, fill in a plan: the product type and strength chosen, as the maker says, and why; the tests the maker requires; and the order of application. Each member then does one stage while the assessor watches: section the dry hair into four; apply base cream to the whole scalp or to the hairline and ears, as the product needs; apply the relaxer in thin partings, starting in the most resistant area and a short distance from the scalp, as the maker says, then the scalp area and ends, with the hairline last; smooth gently; and keep the timer from the first application. Rinse thoroughly with warm water, directing water away from the face, use the neutralising shampoo as the maker says, condition and style with low heat. Photograph each stage (hair and hands only).
materials: Training head with natural, coily, untreated hair, on a clamp
Relaxer or texturiser, with the maker's instructions and SDS (activator if it is a no-lye product)
Neutralising (normalising) shampoo and a conditioner for chemically treated hair
Chemical-resistant gloves, aprons, chemical capes and towels
Tint bowl, applicator brush, tail comb, sectioning clips and a timer

checklist: Helped choose a product and strength from the hair analysis and the maker's instructions
Sectioned dry hair neatly into four
Applied base cream correctly for the product used
Mixed any activator just before use, as the maker says
Applied in thin partings in the correct order, with the hairline last
Smoothed gently without pulling and kept within the maker's time
Rinsed thoroughly and used the neutralising shampoo as the maker says
Conditioned, styled with low heat, and disposed of leftover product and cleaned tools correctly
safety: Follow the maker's instructions, the SDS and the Centre's rules; never mix brands or thio and hydroxide products
Wear chemical-resistant gloves and an apron; keep the area ventilated
Keep relaxer away from eyes; know where the eyewash and clean running water are
Throw away leftover mixed relaxer as the maker says; never save it
Wipe spills at once and keep the floor dry
